checked.what: Overlap with the ground state from the energy, and overlap of two states close to a third
checked.note: Proved as stated; a slip in the printed proof of the second lemma does not affect its statement.

checked.what: Trimming at one cut does not raise the Schmidt rank at any other cut
checked.note: Proved as stated, for every choice of the kept Schmidt terms.

checked.what: Gluing a left half to the right half of a state through its boundary contraction
checked.note: Proved in slightly greater generality, with the factor n of the energy bound replaced by the norm of the terms across and right of the cut.

entries.result: Theorem 1, dependence of the running time on the ground energy
entries.title: Ground energy in the exponent of the running time
entries.summary: Theorem 1 gives an exponent independent of the ground energy, but the normalization of the sampled projector is polynomial in n only when ε0/ε is bounded. The viable-set induction is proved with the sampled projector under such a bound, and without it with Huang's Gaussian filter in place of the sampled projector; on the Gaussian route the running time is stated in the cost model of the note on the cost model.
entries.context: The algorithm uses the operator A = ((1 − H/n)/(1 − ε0/n))m with m of order (n/ε) log n, and samples it by an average of words in the factors 1 − Hi multiplied by Cm, C = (1 − ε0/n)−1. The size of Cm controls the variance in the matrix Bernstein bound, and hence the number of sampled words.
entries.claims: Theorem 1 of arXiv:1307.5143v1 (lines 213–216 of the source) runs in time nc(d, ε) poly(n/η) with c(d, ε) = 2O(log3 d/ε), with no dependence on the ground energy ε0. The proof of the sampling estimate (line 644) uses C2m = nO(1/ε).
entries.found: Cm = (1 − ε0/n)−m is about eε0m/n = nO(ε0/ε). The hypotheses 0 ≤ Hi ≤ 1 allow ε0 of order n, and then this factor, and with it the exponent of the running time, grows with n. Rescaling the sampled operator, which the source allows, does not change the relative accuracy that the number of samples must reach. The corrected exponent is 2O(log3 d/ε) + O(ε0/ε).
entries.impact: The algorithm is polynomial-time whenever ε<sub>0</sub>/ε is bounded, in particular for frustration-free chains; for an extensive ground energy the stated bound does not give polynomial time. The existence statements behind the algorithm do not depend on this: with Huang's Gaussian filter the induction holds under the paper's hypotheses alone.
entries.plan: The note records the failure and corrected statement. For precision c/n<sup>s</sup> and B ≥ ε<sub>0</sub>/ε, explicit intercept and slope constants now prove that the total cut-factor degree is at most p<sub>int</sub> + p<sub>slope</sub>⌈B⌉. This dependence is carried through a complete viable-set step and the induction; the final MPS degree is proved at most (2p<sub>int</sub> + d<sub>0</sub>) + 2p<sub>slope</sub>⌈B⌉. The total number of retained candidates over all cuts and the number of boundary-constrained minimization problems at each cut are also proved polynomial. The support projection for each density optimization has rank at most |S|m, an isometry from at most |S|m coordinates with precisely this range is constructed, and every supported positive-semidefinite density is proved to be the isometric expansion of a positive-semidefinite matrix in those coordinates. Trace, the energy objective, and the trace-norm boundary constraint are transported to the compressed matrix, with the boundary marginal given by an explicit linear map. Every normalized supported eigenvector is likewise transported to at most |S|m coordinates, satisfies the compressed eigenvalue equation, and is recovered by one isometric matrix-vector multiplication; approximate eigenvalue residual norms are preserved exactly. A trace-norm error ε in the compressed density changes trace by at most ε, energy by at most ‖K‖ε, and boundary tolerance by at most ε. A positive approximate solution can be normalized to an exact density within twice its error and then expanded, with energy error 2‖K‖ε and boundary tolerance η+2ε; equivalently its one-sided objective and boundary constraints acquire exactly these slacks. Isometric compression does not increase the objective norm, so these bounds are independent of the coordinate choice. The leading-vector lemma now accepts an arbitrary additive objective error ξ and carries it into the total error e+ξ+‖K‖τ, uniformly for every unit eigenvector with eigenvalue above 1/2. Replacing an exact unit witness by a numerical unit vector within distance ζ costs at most 2‖H‖ζ in energy and ζ in ground-state overlap, hence at most 4Lζ in energy for a normalized range-one chain. The full viable-vector conclusion remains unchanged when the additional boundary error δ satisfies 2(ξ+‖B‖δ) ≤ Δ/2028. These results are composed end to end: a positive compressed density within ε of an exact feasible solution and a normalized numerical eigenvector of the resulting compressed density with residual at most 11ζ/24 produce the physical viable vector whenever 24Lε + 4Lζ ≤ Δ/2028. Isometric expansion preserves norm and residual exactly and enforces the retained-support condition automatically. Independent sufficient targets are ε ≤ Δ/(97344L), ζ ≤ Δ/(16224L), and residual at most 11Δ/(389376L). The leading-vector power method now has n deterministic coordinate starts, one with squared leading overlap at least 1/n. At μ ≥ 23/24, inverse-eigenvalue scaling fixes the leading vector, contracts the orthogonal component by 1/23 per iteration, and gives a nonzero normalized phase-aligned output with an explicit 23<sup>−2t</sup> squared-error bound. Without fixed B the existence construction uses Huang's Gaussian filter. The explicit choice t = ⌈n/ζ²⌉ now meets the LVV vector tolerance and is composed directly with the viable-vector certificate; at the allocated tolerance Lean proves t < n(778752L)²/(11Δ)² + 1 and fewer than n times this many matrix–vector iterations over all coordinate starts. What remains open is the finite-precision numerical arithmetic cost of approximately solving each compressed convex program to the stated trace-norm accuracy.

entries.result: Lemma constantbondapprox, the constant bond dimension
entries.title: A constant bond dimension with different constants
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong with the paper; the formalization proves a bond dimension independent of the chain length and of the cut, of the same form as the paper's, but with constants taken from the area law already in TNLean rather than the dependence on log3 d/ε quoted from Arad, Kitaev, Landau and Vazirani.
entries.context: At a single cut, trimming the ground state Γ to its Bδ largest Schmidt terms and normalizing gives a state with overlap at least 1 − δ with Γ. The algorithm takes δ = cε, and the size of its net of boundary contractions is polynomial in n because Bδ does not depend on n.
entries.claims: For every cut and every δ, the source (lines 342–345) states, without proof and quoting earlier area laws, a bond dimension Bδ = exp(O(ε−1 log3 d log(1/δ))) with this property.
entries.found: From the tail bound on the Schmidt coefficients in the one-dimensional area law of the library, the bond dimension ⌊exp(C + 32s log(2ee/2/δ))⌋ works for every δ > 0, where C bounds the entropy of an interval and s depends on the local dimension and the gap. Like the source's, it is the exponential of an affine function of log(1/δ), independent of n and of the cut; its constants are different. In the size-trimming step, the union over all actual bond dimensions up to D = Bcε multiplies the size of the set by (D + 1)D instead of D, which avoids extending a bond beyond the dimension of the right half.
entries.impact: None for the existence statements. The later steps use only that Bδ is independent of n and of the cut, so the different constant changes the explicit running time, not the conclusions.
entries.plan: The physical per-cut approximation, overlap conversion, linear log(1/δ) rank exponent, and its passage to the actual sequential MPS are proved. AKLV's preceding estimate O(s(log d + log(s²+s))) with s = O(log² d/ε) retains log(1/ε) unless the gap is fixed. Direct physical theorems now supply both normalized same-cut approximants and the actual sequential matrix product state with the printed log³ d dependence uniformly on every interval ε₀ ≤ ε ≤ 1, with an explicit constant depending on the positive lower bound ε₀. A further Lean theorem proves that no universal constant can make this comparison uniformly as ε₀ tends to zero, already for d = 2. Closing the unrestricted gap therefore requires a genuinely sharper rank estimate.

entries.result: Lemma l:leading, chains with at least one site and two states per site
entries.title: Chains with at least one site and two states per site
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong with the paper; the boundary-contraction and leading-vector proof is used for nonempty chains with local dimension at least two. The one-state local space and the empty chain are both handled directly by exact singleton size trimming.
entries.context: The size-trimming step needs an upper bound on the gap, ε ≤ 4, for a nearest-neighbour Hamiltonian with terms of norm at most one; this bound fixes the size of the constant cε = (ε/169)2 relative to ε and the energy error in the leading-vector argument.
entries.claims: The source states the convex program (lines 472–476) and Lemma l:leading (lines 493–505) for every chain of n qudits of dimension d.
entries.found: The upper bound on the gap needs a second state per site and at least one site. In either excluded case the relevant chain and left Hilbert spaces are one-dimensional, so exact size trimming follows directly: viability forces a nonzero family member, and its singleton spans the left Hilbert space. The empty-chain statement avoids the meaningless quantities cε/n and cε/(2n).
entries.impact: None. Both degenerate cases have direct statements giving a singleton family with exact viability and unchanged bond bound.
entries.plan: Resolved: use the boundary-contraction theorem for n ≥ 1 and d ≥ 2, and the direct singleton theorems in the two degenerate cases.

entries.result: Lemma l:trim1, the number of Schmidt terms kept
entries.title: Too few Schmidt terms in the bond-trimming lemma
entries.summary: The printed lemma is false; keeping D/η2 Schmidt terms instead of D/η restores it, and the corrected lemma is proved.
entries.context: Trimming a vector u at a cut keeps its largest Schmidt terms there. The bond-trimming step of the algorithm trims every member of the viable set and needs to know how much overlap with a vector v of Schmidt rank D is lost.
entries.claims: Keeping D/η terms loses at most η: |⟨trim(u), v⟩| ≥ |⟨u, v⟩| − η (lines 531–542). The proof bounds a tail of Schmidt coefficients by η where the argument gives only η2.
entries.found: Take u with (k + 1)D equal Schmidt coefficients and v the normalized sum of its last D Schmidt terms, with η = 1/k. Keeping kD = D/η terms removes v entirely, so the trimmed overlap is zero, while the overlap before trimming is √(η/(1 + η)) > η for η < (√5 − 1)/2. The correct loss after keeping k terms is at most ‖u‖ ‖v‖ √(D/(k + 1)), from Ky Fan's maximum principle, so D/η2 terms suffice.
entries.impact: Only a polynomial changes. In the bond-trimming claim, trimming every bond with loss 1/(48n) needs (48n)2r(n) terms instead of 48n r(n), which is still a polynomial in n.
entries.plan: Use the corrected radius in the bond-trimming claim of the viable-set induction.

entries.result: Lemma l:2, energy of a trimmed low-energy state
entries.title: Energy bound after trimming at one cut
entries.summary: The printed proof does not give the bound ε0 + 6√δ; a corrected bound, which depends on 1/ε, is proved, and the algorithm keeps the source's constant cε by comparing its witness directly with the trimmed ground state.
entries.context: Lemma l:2 trims a state w of energy at most ε0 + δ to the constant Schmidt rank Bδ at one cut and bounds the energy of the normalized result. The algorithm uses such a trimmed state as the good low-rank state at a cut, and chooses its accuracy constant cε = (ε/169)2 from this bound.
entries.claims: If δ(1 + 1/ε) ≤ 1/2, the normalized trimmed state has energy at most ε<sub>0</sub> + 6√δ (lines 347–359).
entries.found: The proof drops the factor 2 of the overlap lemma, uses the Eckart–Young bound for the norm of the trimmed vector as a bound on its square, and loses a term t = 1 − ‖trim w‖2 while writing 2√δ for 2√δ′ with δ′ ≥ δ. Keeping these terms gives the energy bound ε0 + (δ + 2√(2η))/(1 − 2η) with η = 2δ(1 + 1/ε), which grows like √(δ/ε). No counterexample to the printed bound is known. For the ground state itself, the bound ε0 + 6√δ holds for every δ > 0.
entries.impact: No. In the lemma on a trimmed witness, comparing the witness directly with the trimmed ground state avoids the factor 1/ε, so the formalization keeps cε = (ε/169)2 and the energy ε0 + 6√cε. Through Lemma l:2 alone one would need a smaller constant, such as 10−5 min(ε, 1)3, which changes only constants.
entries.plan: Nothing further; the corrected bound and the direct comparison are both proved.

entries.result: Lemma l:constantbondapprox, the net of boundary contractions
entries.title: Size of the net of boundary contractions
entries.summary: The printed size of the net is too small; the correct size, with exponent 2(Bd)2 in place of 2Bd, is proved and is still polynomial in n.
entries.context: A boundary contraction is a density matrix on the site next to the cut and a bond of dimension B, so a matrix of dimension Bd. The algorithm solves one convex problem for each point of a finite net of these matrices in trace norm.
entries.claims: With a grid of step ⌊η/(Bd)2⌋ on [−1, 1], a net of at most (2⌈Bd/η⌉ + 1)2Bd matrices is within trace-norm distance η of every matrix of trace norm at most one (lines 451–460).
entries.found: The floor makes the step zero for small η, so the step is read as η/(Bd)2, and the net is named for δ where η is meant. A complex matrix of dimension Bd has 2(Bd)2 real coordinates, and covering the unit ball needs at least η−2(Bd)2 balls of radius η, so the printed size fails once Bd ≥ 2 and η is small. Rounding every coordinate to the grid gives a net of at most (2⌈(Bd)2/η⌉ + 1)2(Bd)2 points. The distance estimate holds as printed.
entries.impact: None for polynomial time. At η = cε/(2n) the corrected size is still polynomial in n, with exponent 2(Bcεd)2.
entries.plan: The corrected net is proved and is used in the size-trimming step on the chain.

entries.result: Lemma l:within, energy of a viable-set witness
entries.title: A factor two in the energy of a witness
entries.summary: One inference in the proof of Lemma l:within omits a factor two, which changes a constant and nothing else; the corrected inference is proved.
entries.context: A witness for a viable set is a state with overlap at least 1 − δ with Γ whose left half is supported on the span of the set. Lemma l:within needs a bound on its energy to produce a good low-rank state supported on that span.
entries.claims: A unit witness with overlap at least 1 − cε/n with Γ, for a Hamiltonian of norm at most n, has energy at most ε0 + cε (lines 509–515).
entries.found: The excess energy is at most ‖H − ε0‖(1 − |⟨Γ, v⟩|2), and an overlap of at least 1 − δ gives 1 − |⟨Γ, v⟩|2 ≤ 2δ, so the bound is ε0 + 2cε. A diagonal two-by-two Hamiltonian shows that the factor two cannot be removed from this inference.
entries.impact: No. The later steps absorb the larger excess; on the chain the witness is shown to have energy at most ε0 + 8cε, and the trimmed witness still has energy at most ε0 + 6√cε.
entries.plan: Nothing further; the corrected estimate is used in the lemma on a trimmed witness.

entries.result: Claim c:errorreduction, the decomposition of a word across a cut
entries.title: Paired indices in the decomposition of the crossing term
entries.summary: The printed decomposition of the term across the cut has independent indices, which would make it a single product; pairing the indices gives the stated count of d2 terms, and the corrected bound is proved.
entries.context: To apply the sampled projector to a viable set, each word in the factors 1 − Hj is written as a sum of products of an operator left of the cut and one right of it. Only 1 − Hi crosses the cut (i, i + 1), and each occurrence of it is expanded into d2 such products.
entries.claims: 1 − Hi = ∑j,k=1d Ej ⊗ Fk (line 584), so that a word with k occurrences of it is a sum of at most d2k products.
entries.found: A double sum with independent indices factors as (∑ Ej) ⊗ (∑ Fk), a single product, which a general two-site operator is not: the positive contraction |00⟩⟨00| + |11⟩⟨11| needs two products, and it occurs in a gapped chain with positive terms. Writing the operator through its blocks Eab ⊗ Bab, with both factors indexed by the same pair (a, b), gives d2 terms, and the bound d2k for a word follows.
entries.impact: None; the count used by the algorithm is the corrected one.
entries.plan: Nothing further; the bound on the operator Schmidt rank of an ordered word is proved for any finite set of sites.

entries.result: Equation eq:a-exp, the expansion of the power projector
entries.title: The n-th letter of the power expansion is the identity
entries.summary: The expansion of the power projector into words sums over n letters although the Hamiltonian has n − 1 terms; reading the extra letter as the identity makes the identity exact, and the formal statement uses that reading.
entries.context: The operator A = Cm(1 − H/n)m, with C = (1 − ε0/n)−1, is expanded as an average over words in the factors Pi = 1 − Hi, so that it can later be sampled word by word.
entries.claims: A = Cm n−m ΣI ∈ {1,…,n}m PI, with PI the ordered product of the letters of I (lines 606–609).
entries.found: H has only the terms H1, …, Hn−1, so Pn is undefined. With Hn = 0, that is Pn = 1, the letters sum to n − H and the identity holds exactly. The extra letter acts on no site, so it never crosses a cut and leaves the rank estimate unchanged.
entries.impact: None; the expansion, the spectral bounds and the rank estimate hold as stated with this reading.
entries.plan: Nothing further; the reading is part of the formal definition of the letters.

entries.result: Claim c:2, the net point in the leading-vector lemma
entries.title: The net point in the leading-vector lemma
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong with the paper; the leading-vector theorem was first proved for an arbitrary boundary point near the actual one, and the size-trimming theorem now combines it with the net and its polynomial size.
entries.context: Lemma l:leading takes the point of the net of boundary contractions closest to that of a good low-rank state, solves the convex program at that point, and shows that the leading eigenvector of the solution is a good left half. Claim c:2 bounds the size of the resulting set by the size of the net.
entries.claims: The net point is the element of the net nearest the boundary contraction of the good state (lines 493–495), and the size of the set is at most the size of the net times the bond dimension (lines 519–520).
entries.found: The leading-vector theorem holds for every boundary point within the tolerance of the convex program, which includes the nearest net point but makes no assertion about the net. The size-trimming theorem chooses a net for every actual bond dimension, solves the program at every point of it before the ground state is known, and shows that the resulting set has polynomial size and contains a good left half whenever its input is viable. The note recording this gap predates that theorem and still describes it as open.
entries.impact: None; Claim c:2 is proved, with the constant-bond restriction recorded separately and both degenerate chain cases handled by exact singleton reductions.
entries.plan: Update the note to record that the size-trimming theorem closes the gap.

entries.title: Bond dimension at most zero is read as at most one
entries.summary: A degenerate case of the definition of a viable set is read as the authors intend; nothing is wrong with the paper, and the extension step is proved for every bond dimension.
entries.context: A viable set of bond dimension b consists of matrix product states with bonds of dimension at most b. The extension step tensors every member with the basis states of the next site and keeps the same b.
entries.claims: Appending one site in a basis state does not raise the bond dimension (line 399).
entries.found: A vector on one site has no internal bond, so its bond dimension is zero, while a nonzero product vector on two sites has a bond of dimension one. The source uses b = 0 only for the initial set {1} at the start of the sweep (line 372), and its later bond dimensions are positive polynomials. The formalization reads a bond dimension of at most b as at most max(1, b).
entries.impact: None; every bound with b ≥ 1 is unchanged.
entries.plan: Nothing further; the convention is part of the definition.

entries.title: The error-reduction step needs a lower bound on the norm of A v
entries.summary: The passage from A v to K v in the proof of the error-reduction claim needs a lower bound on ‖A v‖; the source's A supplies ‖A v‖ ≥ 1/2, and the new error is δ + 4‖K − A‖ in place of 2δ, a change of constant that the free polynomial q(n) absorbs.
entries.context: Error reduction applies the left factors Aj of a decomposition K = Σj Aj ⊗ Bj of the sampled projector to a half-viable set. A witness v of the old set is mapped to the witness K v/‖K v‖ of the new one.
entries.claims: From |⟨Γ, A v/‖A v‖⟩| ≥ 1 − δ and ‖K − A‖ ≤ δ it follows that |⟨Γ, K v/‖K v‖⟩| ≥ 1 − 2δ (line 589).
entries.found: Without a lower bound on ‖A v‖ the implication fails: in ℂ2 with Γ = v = e1, A = δ·1 and K = A + δ|e2⟩⟨e1|, the overlap of K v/‖K v‖ with Γ is 1/√2. The source's A is Hermitian and fixes Γ (line 602), so ‖A v‖ ≥ |⟨Γ, v⟩| ≥ 1/2, and the triangle inequality gives 1 − δ − 4‖K − A‖.
entries.impact: None for the claim, which is stated for an arbitrary polynomial q(n); a smaller sampling error restores the printed target error.
entries.plan: Nothing further; the deterministic error-reduction step is proved with the corrected constant.

entries.result: Theorem t:mcb, the variance parameter of the matrix Bernstein bound
entries.title: The variance parameter of the matrix Bernstein bound
entries.summary: The quoted matrix Bernstein bound takes the maximum of two matrices as its variance; read as the maximum of their norms, as in Tropp's theorem from which it is derived, the bound is proved.
entries.context: The sampled projector is an average of independent random matrices, and the matrix Bernstein bound controls how far such an average lies from its mean in operator norm. Its variance parameter measures the spread of a single sample.
entries.claims: Theorem t:mcb of arXiv:1307.5143v1 (lines 616–624 of the source) defines σ2 as the maximum of the two positive semidefinite matrices E(Xi − X)(Xi − X)* and E(Xi − X)*(Xi − X), and places σ2 in a scalar exponent.
entries.found: Two positive semidefinite matrices have no maximum in general, and a matrix cannot stand in the exponent. Tropp's rectangular inequality, from which the bound is derived, uses the larger of the two operator norms; with that reading the printed bound, with dimension factor 2d, follows.
entries.impact: A notational slip; the bound used by the sampled projector is unchanged.
entries.plan: Resolved: the bound with the norm reading is proved in QICLean and used by the sampled projector.

entries.result: Lemma l:mpsapprox, the sub-polynomial bond dimension
entries.title: A logarithmic factor in the sub-polynomial bond dimension
entries.summary: The paper quotes the bond dimension exp(C(ln n)3/4ε−1/4) without the tilde of its source, Arad, Kitaev, Landau and Vazirani; their bound, with the hidden factor written out as log log n, is proved.
entries.context: The area law shows that the ground state is close to a matrix product state of small bond dimension. The algorithm needs only a polynomial bond dimension, but the paper states the best known one as a lemma.
entries.claims: Lemma l:mpsapprox of arXiv:1307.5143v1 (lines 325–328 of the source): for every c > 0 there is C such that some vector of Schmidt rank at most exp(C(ln n)3/4ε−1/4) at every cut has overlap at least 1 − n−c with Γ.
entries.found: The cited work, arXiv:1301.1162v1, states B = eÕ(log3/4 n/ε1/4) (lines 176 and 1503–1517), where the tilde hides factors logarithmic in the exponent. Its derivation balances two terms and leaves a factor of order log log n.
entries.impact: None for the algorithm, which uses only a polynomial bond dimension. The lemma is formalized in the form its source proves.
entries.plan: Resolved: a matrix product state with log D = O((log n)3/4 log log n) for fixed local dimension and gap, at accuracy 1/poly(n), is proved.

entries.result: Theorem 1, the cost model of the running time
entries.title: The cost model of the running time
entries.summary: The algorithm is a computation over linear-algebra operations, each charged a declared polynomial cost in the dimensions of its arguments; run with any valid oracle (a solver returning optimal solutions of the convex programs, nets of the required radius and cut decompositions of the filters) it computes a viable sweep, outputs a matrix product state with the required overlap, and costs at most P(n + 2R2 + 1)d. The costs and exact arithmetic are declared, not derived, as in the source.
entries.context: Theorem 1 (lines 213–219 of the source) counts each linear-algebra step, the matrix elements in an orthonormal basis of the span, the convex programs, the singular value decompositions and the leading eigenvectors, as one polynomial-time computation on data of polynomial dimension, and does not analyse it further.
entries.claims: The algorithm runs in time nc(d, ε) poly(n/η) and outputs a matrix product state with overlap at least 1 − η with the ground state.
entries.impact: The running time is a statement about declared costs and the honest oracle; the exponent 2O(log3 d/ε) is not reproduced, since the library's constant-cut bond differs from the source's.
entries.plan: The declaration of costs is the content of the source's claim. The honest-oracle restriction is lifted for correctness on both routes and for the success probability of the sampled route. The cost bound holds for every valid oracle on both routes; on the sampled route it holds on the same event of probability at least 1 − 1/(2n2) as the accuracy.
